Ioannina New Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Ioannina, Greece

Not demolished. Jews first settled in Ioannina in the early centuries CE, forming a sizable Romaniot community by the 14th century that remained Greece's largest and oldest of its kind, since arriving Sephardi refugees largely assimilated into it. Sephardi Jews formed their own congregation in 1540; the Romaniot congregation built a magnificent synagogue in 1824 (still standing today), matched by an equally grand Sephardi building in 1841, alongside a separate Sicilian congregation. Population reached 2,400 by 1856; two devastating 1867 fires left 840 Jews homeless, prompting emigration to Egypt, the Land of Israel, and the US. From 1865, Alliance Israelite education efforts culminated in a school opening in 1904, the same year population peaked at 4,000; two Zionist associations followed (1905, 1909). Postwar emigration to the US, Turkey, France, and the Land of Israel continued; by 1928, Ioannina was Greece's third-largest Jewish community (1,970) after Salonika and Kavala. The era's greatest Greek-language Jewish poet, Yosef Eliyia, lived there during this period, alongside a growing social welfare network including an old age home. Population reached 1,950 by 1941; many Ioannina Jews fought against Italian forces on the Albanian border during WWII. On March 24, 1944, Germans rounded up roughly 1,870 Jews, deporting them via Trikala and Larissa to Auschwitz-Birkenau - only 164 survived. The community revived postwar but remained small. This cemetery's founding is unknown, presumed 19th century, serving both the Romaniot and Sephardi communities together.
